title: North American Winter Precipitation Extremes: Changes in Variability and Driving Mechanisms in a Warming Climate
content:
Abstract

Multiday winter extreme precipitation across North America (NA) has become more frequent and intense, posing hydrological and socioeconomic risks. This study examines changes in dominant spatial patterns of monthly maximum 5-day precipitation (Rx5day) during the extended winter (November–March) between the historical (1961–2010) and future (2051–2100) periods under three Shared Socioeconomic Pathway emissions pathways. The analysis uses a multi-model ensemble of 32 global climate models, including two 30-member initial-condition ensembles. Three distinct modes of Rx5day variability are identified using a common empirical orthogonal function (EOF) approach. Historical Rx5day variability is driven by large-scale circulations extending from the North Pacific to the North Atlantic, which modulate atmospheric moisture transport and extreme precipitation over NA. Future projections indicate statistically significant increases in both the mean and variability of Rx5day across NA, with larger increases over eastern regions and amplified changes in EOF patterns under higher emission scenarios. Projected changes in tropical and subtropical Pacific sea surface temperatures modify the subtropical jet, altering the dynamical and thermodynamical conditions conducive to extreme precipitation. Moisture flux convergence is primarily driven by transient wind systems interacting with the background moisture field, reflecting the critical role of synoptic-scale dynamics. Internal climate variability and model structural uncertainty have comparable influences on Rx5day variability and associated drivers in both historical and future periods. These findings advance understanding of winter extreme precipitation variability over NA, revealing increased complexity and regional heterogeneity driven by changes in large-scale atmospheric circulation and associated shifts in moisture transport under future warming.
